passage: Nursery note, Monday. When I crouched down, arms loose in my lap, and said “Come and see the puzzle”, Vandana, two, walked right over and climbed on my knee. Then our supervisor came to the door, standing tall with arms folded, saying something friendly about the weather. Vandana stopped, edged back and held on to my sleeve. I said nothing, but I kept her close, and asked the supervisor to crouch down and greet her slowly. She smiled at last. 🙂 Payal

qa.q: Where did Vandana go when I crouched down?
qa.a: She walked over and climbed on Payal's knee.

qa.q: Why did Vandana edge back when the supervisor arrived?
qa.a: She was probably reacting to the tall, stiff stance, which feels threatening to a small child. She might also have been surprised by a new person, since the words were friendly.

qa.q: What could Payal and the supervisor do differently in future?
qa.a: They could crouch to the child's height and keep their bodies open and relaxed when greeting a toddler.

qa.q: How might the supervisor feel when Vandana backs away?
qa.a: The supervisor may feel puzzled, thinking they were friendly, until she learns that a toddler reads posture before words.

grounding: A toddler reacts to a caregiver's stance, feeling safe with a crouched open posture and threatened by a stiff looming one.

passage: Chinmay came in from the field after a long day, shoulders hard and jaw tight, standing in the doorway with his hands on his hips. His son Eshaan, two, who had been playing with pebbles, stopped and stayed where he was, watching. Chinmay noticed. He breathed out, walked to the mat, sat down and let his arms rest on his knees. “Come, Eshaan.” Eshaan crept toward him, dropped a pebble in his palm and climbed onto his lap.

qa.q: Where did Chinmay sit down to invite Eshaan?
qa.a: On the mat, with his arms resting on his knees.

qa.q: Why might Eshaan have stayed where he was at first?
qa.a: He was probably reading his father's tight, standing posture as tense, though he might simply have been focused on his pebbles.

qa.q: What could Chinmay do when he comes home tired?
qa.a: He could pause at the door, soften his body and get down to Eshaan's level before speaking.

qa.q: What might Chinmay feel when Eshaan holds back?
qa.a: He might feel a pang or surprise at his son's caution, and then understand that his tired body sent a message.

grounding: A toddler notices a caregiver's stance, reacting cautiously to a tense standing posture and approaching a lowered, open one.

passage:
The paint pot tipped over, and red spread across the kitchen floor in Haifa. Noa stood over it, tall and stiff, hands on hips. "Yara!"
Yara shrank back against the cupboard, shoulders up, eyes on her mother's body, not her face.
Noa noticed. She let out a breath, crouched down low and opened her arms. "It's okay. Come." Yara hesitated, then stepped into the hug, red footprints and all.

qa.q: What colour was the paint that spilled?
qa.a: Red.

qa.q: What was Yara feeling when she shrank back against the cupboard?
qa.a: She was frightened by her mother's tall, stiff stance, reading it as a threat before understanding any words.

qa.q: What did Noa change, and why did it help?
qa.a: She crouched low and opened her arms, a safe, open posture that told Yara she was not in danger.

qa.q: How might Noa feel after seeing Yara shrink back?
qa.a: She might feel a pang of regret, realising her stance scared Yara more than the words did.

grounding: A toddler shrinks from her mother's stiff, looming stance and comes to her when she crouches with open arms.

passage: I'm Hafsa, and I took my little brother Bhupen for his check-up. When the doctor stood right over him, tall in a white coat, Bhupen pressed his face into my side and wouldn't look. Then the nurse came and knelt on the floor, hands open, smiling. Bhupen peeked. He stared at her a long time. Then he held out his arm for her to look at. I can't say what changed for him. Maybe it was just her kneeling.

qa.q: What did the nurse do when she came in?
qa.a: She knelt on the floor with her hands open, smiling.

qa.q: What might Bhupen have been feeling when the doctor stood over him?
qa.a: He was likely scared of the tall figure looming over him; the nurse kneeling seems to have made him feel safer and more curious.

qa.q: What could the doctor learn from the nurse?
qa.a: Getting down to a child's level with an open posture can help a small child feel safe enough to cooperate.

qa.q: How does Hafsa experience the check-up?
qa.a: Hafsa feels her brother pressed against her side and is unsure what changed, noticing it might have been the kneeling.

grounding: A sister sees her toddler brother hide from a standing doctor and relax toward a kneeling nurse.

passage:
Monday: Anjali came home tense from a phone call and stood stiffly at the door. Bhavna hung back, watching, and didn't run to her as usual.
Wednesday: Anjali crouched down in the doorway and opened her arms. Bhavna ran straight in.
The next Monday: Bhavna headed for the stairs. Anjali crouched, arms open, and said, "Not the stairs, come here." Bhavna turned and came, without tears.

qa.q: What did Anjali do in the doorway on Wednesday?
qa.a: She crouched down and opened her arms.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna hang back on Monday?
qa.a: She was likely uneasy because her mother stood stiffly and tense, which felt unsafe even though no words were said.

qa.q: Which of Anjali's changes worked, and why?
qa.a: Crouching with open arms worked, because Bhavna read the lower, relaxed posture as safe, even when hearing "no".

qa.q: How might Anjali feel when Bhavna comes away from the stairs without tears?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and encouraged that her posture made a hard "no" easier. 🙂

grounding: Over a week a mother learns that her toddler reads her posture before her words, and uses a lowered, open stance.

passage:
Blue paint spread across the floor of the Aizawl flat. Kamal stood beside the tipped pot, hands blue to the wrists.
Lalremsiami came in and stopped, standing tall over him, hands on her hips. “Kamal!”
Kamal froze. His eyes fixed on her; his chin started to shake.
She saw his face and let out a breath. She knelt down, dropped her shoulders and opened her hands. “Oops. Paint everywhere. Let's clean it together.”
Kamal took a slow step towards her.

qa.q: What colour was the paint on the floor?
qa.a: The paint was blue.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling when Lalremsiami stood over him with hands on her hips?
qa.a: He was frightened by her looming, tense stance, as his freezing and shaking chin show, even before he understood her words.

qa.q: What changed Kamal's reaction, and why?
qa.a: Lalremsiami knelt, relaxed her shoulders and opened her hands; the lower, open posture felt safe, so he stepped towards her.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel when she saw Kamal's face?
qa.a: She let out a breath, which suggests she calmed her own irritation when she saw he was scared.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler reacting to a parent's looming, tense stance with fear and relaxing when she kneels in an open, lowered posture.
